The Head of Cybersecurity Technology Standards at Ghana’s Cyber Security Authority (CSA), Jake France, has called for a real-time communications platform to enable banks, telecommunications companies, fintechs, regulators and other players in Ghana’s digital finance ecosystem share information on cyber incidents and emerging threats.
The platform would help institutions alert one another quickly when breaches or fraudulent activities occur, allowing others in the ecosystem to assess their exposure and take appropriate action. The call reflects growing concerns that as digital financial services become increasingly interconnected, a security breach in one institution can have consequences for several others.
“I believe a real-time communication platform which collates all the information for the sectors and the regulator to participate in is necessary,” he said, adding, “If we had one platform where all these institutions could report their breaches in real-time and we also had visibility of it, it would be easier to look at some of these issues and triage them in consultation with all the stakeholders. Unfortunately, we’re not there yet but that is the ultimate dream.”
He cautioned that delays in reporting could expose more organisations to an attack because intelligence about a breach could not be disseminated quickly enough. A common platform, he stressed, should not serve as “a security camera looking at everybody’s transactions”, but as a means of rapidly communicating breaches and suspicious activity so institutions could assess their own environments and respond.
He made the call during a UK-Ghana Chamber of Commerce (UKGCC) and EY Ghana webinar on “Securing Ghana’s Digital Finance Ecosystem: From Institutional Silos to Building Collective Cyber Resilience.”
The other panellists, including Elikplim Kitsikpui, Lead in EY Ghana's Digital Technology Consulting team; Joy Aigbe, Head of Cybersecurity at Telecel Ghana; and John Awuah, Chief Executive Officer of the Ghana Association of Banks (GAB), supported the call, emphasising the need for stronger cooperation and faster information exchange among institutions.
Kitsikpui said, “We can’t eliminate cybersecurity attacks, but we can minimise the impact. And to minimise that impact, we need to find a way of creating the platform that Jake spoke about.”
Aigbe similarly prioritised “the establishment of a formal cross-sector cyber coordination and information-sharing platform” bringing together telcos, banks, fintechs, regulators, and relevant law-enforcement bodies. She said it must be operational, enabling participants to exchange intelligence, incident indicators, trends, and mitigation actions in near real time.
John Awuah, in his support of the call, highlighted its urgency saying, “That platform, I can’t say enough that we need it like yesterday.”
For Awuah, the urgency ultimately comes down to public confidence.
“Trust, as we all see, is the currency of the digital finance system,” he remarked, arguing that once trust is compromised, the robustness of a system or the scale of investment in it means little to the customer.
For Aigbe, the growth of Ghana’s digital finance ecosystem has expanded financial inclusion while making institutions increasingly interdependent. This, she said, required a corresponding shift in how cybersecurity risks are managed.
“The question is no longer whether an organisation can protect itself in isolation. The real measure of resilience is now how effectively the entire ecosystem can detect, communicate, and respond together when one part of the system comes under attack,” she said.
She also recommended fraud operations centres within financial institutions to complement their security operations centres and serve as gateways for cross-institution collaboration.
Kitsikpui stressed preparedness. Institutions, he said, should establish cross-institutional incident coordination frameworks, determine beforehand what information can be shared and with whom, define escalation thresholds, and test those arrangements jointly.
“The middle of a cyber crisis is the wrong time to be identifying what to do, what to share, what not to share, and who to call,” he said.
Awuah urged every participant to treat cyber risk with the same seriousness because an attack can rapidly cross institutional boundaries.
“When there is a shared risk, what do you do? You need to have a shared response,” he said, calling for mechanisms that could detect attacks and trace or recover funds even after fraudulent proceeds had moved between banks and other platforms.
The webinar, moderated by Traci Gyebi, a Technology Consultant at EY Ghana, also explored the role of banks and other financial-sector players in detecting, reporting and responding to fraud; emerging threats; customer education; third-party risks; coordinated incident response; and practical measures for building collective cyber resilience.
